summary: Describes the Network Time Protocol, which distributes time information across a large internet. It uses a hierarchy of time servers that synchronize each other. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some computers have very good clocks and share the time with others, which share it with others, like passing a message down a line.

subtitle: How a network keeps accurate time across many computers

tldr.problem: Computers on the Internet have clocks that drift and disagree, making it difficult to coordinate actions, log events reliably or conduct transactions that depend on precise timestamps.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Time Protocol (NTP) uses a hierarchy of time servers synchronized to national time standards via radio or wire, and distributes accurate time to client computers through a robust protocol that filters out bad data and selects the most reliable sources.
tldr.outcome: NTP has been in operation for years and keeps most Internet hosts within tens of milliseconds of Coordinated Universal Time, even when networks fail or individual time servers become unreliable.

today: RFC 1129 is Informational, providing an overview of NTP. The formal specification is in RFC 1119. NTP remains the standard protocol for Internet time synchronization and is widely deployed today.

sections.title: The Problem of Network Time
sections.content:
Most computers have a quartz-crystal clock that drifts several seconds per day. A survey of over 94,000 Internet hosts showed that about half had time errors greater than two minutes, and some had errors of weeks. Yet distributed applications, transactions, and system management all need clocks to agree.

NTP solves this by distributing accurate time from a few reference sources (computers with timecode receivers synchronized to national time standards) through a self-organizing hierarchy of secondary servers and client computers.
sections.eli5: Computer clocks are not very accurate on their own. NTP gets accurate time from a few special clocks and spreads it to all the others.

sections.title: The Synchronization Hierarchy
sections.content:
NTP organizes servers into layers called strata. Stratum 1 servers connect directly to atomic clocks or radio time signals. Stratum 2 servers get their time from Stratum 1, Stratum 3 from Stratum 2, and so on. Each server shares time with multiple sources and uses algorithms to identify which peers are most reliable and accurate.

The protocol runs continuously. Clients or peer servers send timestamp messages to each other; by comparing send and receive times, they calculate the network delay and their clock offset (how far they are from the reference time). These measurements are filtered to improve accuracy despite network jitter.
sections.eli5: The most accurate clocks are at the top. Clocks below them ask those above, and share what they learn with others below them.

sections.title: Reliability and Security
sections.content:
NTP is designed to survive failures. It does not require reliable message delivery; a few lost packets do not hurt. Servers track which peers are reachable and gradually increase the polling interval (time between updates) when a peer is stable, to reduce network load.

The protocol includes optional cryptographic authentication to prevent attackers from forging time data. Special checks detect duplicate messages, out-of-order packets, and bogus timestamps. These mechanisms allow NTP to operate safely even when networks or servers misbehave.
sections.eli5: Even if some messages get lost or someone tries to lie about the time, NTP figures out what is really true by trusting multiple sources.

sections.title: Measured Accuracy
sections.content: The RFC reports that the NTP synchronization subnet operating on the Internet ordinarily maintains accuracy to within tens of milliseconds throughout most of the Internet, even in cases of network failure, clock failure, or disruption. Accuracy degrades gracefully with distance from primary servers and network path quality, but the redundancy and filtering algorithms keep the system reliable.
sections.eli5: In practice, NTP keeps clocks accurate to within a fraction of a second, which is good enough for almost everything.

references.text: Mills, D., "A Specification of the Internet Time Synchronization Protocol (NTP)", RFC 1119, September 1989.
